done.why: The world told me I'd taken all 150 turns it allows. I was mid-maze, holding the coins and the skeleton key, still hunting for whatever that key opens.

about: A reworked Zork: the white house, the trap door that someone bars behind you, a troll who eats whatever you hand him, a small underground of cellar, chasm, gallery and studio, and a tight twisty maze with a dead adventurer in it. It's about poking at a famous old place and finding it talks back with a dry, slightly weary voice; everything outside the maze is quick, and the maze is where the game actually makes you work.

moments.note: Knocking on the boarded door got 'Nobody's home.' The game answers nonsense in kind.
'squeeze through the window' said I couldn't see any such thing, while the window was in the room description.
Poured water into the sack; it 'leaks out and evaporates immediately.' Fine, I asked for it.
'eat the lunch' refused with 'You're not holding that', though reading the leaflet had auto-taken it at turn 5.
The gothic lettering translates to 'This space intentionally left blank.'
Hitting the nailed door with the sword: 'I've known strange people, but fighting a wooden door?'
The trap door crashes shut and someone bars it. Someone. I never found out who.
The troll gleefully eats the garlic, then the glass bottle, then the sack. His appetite had no floor.
Troll description: teeth 'not all of them his own', watching me 'the way a cook watches a chicken'.
Disarmed troll 'appears to have an axe to grind with you.' I groaned happily.
Dead-end wall is 'solid, plain and entirely uninterested in you.'
Came into the dead end heading east, and west wouldn't take me back out.
Thirty-odd turns of bare 'Maze' and 'Dead End' with nothing found, and 'listen' and 'exits' unrecognized.
Down from the sword room is a one-way tunnel: 'You won't be able to get back up.'
'look into the chasm' -> 'You can't look inside a chasm.' A bottomless chasm I can't even peer at.
The painting, 'done with such tenderness that it is hard to look at it for long, and harder to look away.'
Chimney refusal states its rule plainly: me, a light, and one thing more, 'not an inch besides.'
East of the troll room: 'has not been finished. A note is pinned to the rock: Back soon. -- The Management.'
The note is spiked in 'by someone stronger than you.'
Up from a nothing room: the skeleton, his useless lantern, a key, a knife, a bag of coins.
The skeleton 'found the moment longer than expected... the maze found him first.'

wished: Catch or at least hear whoever keeps barring the trap door above me; I'd have waited at the stairs for them if I'd had turns to spare.
A 'listen' or 'exits' verb in the maze, or any description detail beyond 'all alike' to hang a map on.
To look into the chasm, or throw something in and hear it fall.
To take the Management's note, or write back on it.
To find what the skeleton key opens, which I assume is a grating I never reached.

lines.line: The skeleton lies where its owner fell, slumped against the wall of the passage as though he had sat down for a moment's rest and found the moment longer than expected... Whatever he came into the maze looking for, the maze found him first.
lines.why: After forty turns lost in the maze myself, this landed. It's the game admitting what the maze is for.

lines.line: He is watching you the way a cook watches a chicken.
lines.why: One sentence told me exactly what the troll was and that I'd better act.

lines.line: The passage to the east has not been finished. A note is pinned to the rock: "Back soon. -- The Management."
lines.why: The edge of the world turned into a joke instead of a wall. Honest and funny at once.

lines.line: It is a painting of a sunlit valley, done with such tenderness that it is hard to look at it for long, and harder to look away.
lines.why: The one piece of real beauty underground, and the prose rose to it.

lines.line: I've known strange people, but fighting a wooden door?
lines.why: I push on refusals by habit; this one pushed back with a grin.

lines.line: The engravings translate to "This space intentionally left blank."
lines.why: First sign the world would reward reading things that didn't matter.

lines.line: The chimney has room for you, a light to climb by and one thing more, and not an inch besides.
lines.why: A refusal that tells you the rule instead of just saying no. I solved it in one move because of it.

fun.why: Feeding the troll everything I owned, the Management's note, the chimney rule, and the skeleton find were real pleasures. The long stretch of bare 'Maze' rooms between turns 49 and 92 dragged, and the cap landed before the payoff.

engagement.why: I kept wanting the next room, and the barred trap door and glowing sword pulled me downward fast. The maze cost momentum but the one-way tunnel and the skeleton pulled me back in.

difficulty.why: The house and troll were easy; the maze is where all the difficulty lives, and it's dense enough that I burned sixty-plus turns in it and still hadn't found the grating when the cap hit. Right for a maze, hard on a turn budget.

interestingness.why: Who bars the trap door? Who is the Management? Who was the skeleton? The world keeps dropping these and never explains, which I liked. The unfinished east passage being in-fiction is a good idea.

prose.why: Short, dry, and sharp when it wants to be: the troll, the painting, the ramp 'polished smooth by everything that has ever slid down it', the skeleton. The maze rooms are deliberately bare, which hurt. A few stock refusals ('That sentence isn't one I recognize') were flat beside the rest.
